doc.title: John Bunch interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Indiana University, jazz frowned upon, and classical study
summary: He went to Indiana after the war, wasn't admitted to music school, joined Med Flory's band and studied piano on the side.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: And you attended the great Indiana University.
I did, later on, after the war, after World War II, yeah.
Tell us about that. Tell us about the program that was going on at that time.

Well you know they had a great music school, they still have you know. But at that time they frowned on jazz. Jazz was sort of a dirty word in those days, in 1946 or ‘5, whenever it was. And not only that but I wasn’t a very good, legitimate musician. I couldn’t read music very well and didn’t have any classical training, so I wasn’t accepted in music school so I was very disappointed. But I went there anyhow because there was a very good jazz band there that we made, we played a lot of dances, in Med Flory’s band. He’s quite well known right here in Los Angeles. And anyhow, so I wanted to play with his band so I signed up to be a student in speech. I was going to be a radio announcer. I
figured that’s as close as I can get to music. And meanwhile I took piano lessons while I was there on the side you know, to learn to play classical music and read music better.
Did you feel that that helped your overall technique and you were able to blend the two concepts?

Yeah to a certain degree, yeah, to a certain degree. Although, well it’s debatable about that, whether classical music helps your jazz or not. You know Benny Goodman played awful good before he ever took a lot of, studied a lot of classical music, so I’m not so sure that it really helps that much.
